Fortress revival · process engineering · 3 Oct 2026

Batch 10, designed blind

Two designers each wrote a workflow for climb batch 10 from its goals alone. Nothing they wrote was run. This page sets the two designs beside the pipeline batch 10 is running on now.

Reading the numbers

M is a million tokens written: cache writes plus new input, with cached reads not counted. That is the project's unit POSITIONS.

Each number carries a tag naming its file:

  • B9 §nexplorations/reviews/batch-9-review.md
  • Rec §nexplorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-10.md
  • Briefexplorations/coordinator/process-engineering/design-batch10-brief.md
  • Fable §n…/process-engineering/design-batch10-fable.md
  • Opus §n…/process-engineering/design-batch10-opus.md
  • Labor…/process-engineering/labor.md
  • Script :nexplorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js
  • Manualexplorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md
  • POSITIONSexplorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md
  • Heldexplorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md (the boot note)
  1. The question and what ran
  2. How the designers were briefed
  3. The pipeline batch 10 runs on
  4. The two designs
  5. Side by side, role by role
  6. Where the tokens go today
  7. Decisions put to you
  8. What comes next

1The question and what ran

  • The question. What workflow would a designer build for batch 10 from its goals alone, and where would it spend less than ours? In the brief's words: "to see what you would design from the goals alone" Brief.
  • What ran. Two design-only workers, one on Opus and one on Fable, each blind to our pipeline and to the other Held.
  • What each wrote. One document: the design, its Workflow script, how it checks correctness, its cost estimate, and what to measure or decide first Brief.
  • Nothing was built, run or tested. Both designs exist on paper only.
  • Batch 10 runs now on the existing pipeline, launched at 05:27 UTC Held, so its measured cost can be set beside both designs once it lands.

2How the designers were briefed

They got the goals, your binding rules, the machine's costs and a general scripting reference. They did not get our pipeline, but parts of it showed through.

What they were given

  • Batch 10's goals: the record's sections 1 to 5 Brief. These describe four rungs. A rung is one piece of work, done by one worker in its own copy of the tree. W changes walk's (the interpreter's) load-time checks; C repairs the compiled checker's defects; G and N repair one-off slips in two parts of the library Rec §1.
  • Your requirements from POSITIONS, as binding Brief:
    • test first, the test kept in the corpus;
    • the suite's verdict is the check, with no output comparisons;
    • nothing built or run twice on the same code;
    • both full suites green on the merged tree before anything lands (testFast, which holds the compiler tests, and testSystem, the interpreter tests);
    • workers commit only what main is to hold;
    • the specification revised with each change in the S1 form (a marked callout at the passage and an Appendix I entry with the reason);
    • tiers: Opus for workers, Sonnet for archaeology (reading history, transcripts and logs), Fable, the top tier with its own scarcer weekly pool, only for judgements;
    • costs in tokens written.
  • The machine's costs Brief: 4 CPUs; two agents at a time; about 45K tokens before an agent does anything; a prompt cache that lives 5 minutes, so a longer wait rewrites the agent's whole context; a built tree copied into a new worktree in about 3 s; the session stopped after about 13 hours; past batches wrote about 6M to 8M each.
  • The workflow-authoring skill, described next.

The workflow-authoring skill

  • It is a reference for writing Workflow scripts: how agents are started, chained and run in parallel, how a stopped run resumes, and the traps.
  • It also lists general quality patterns: several skeptics trying to refute a finding, a panel of judges, searching until a round finds nothing new, a last critic asking what is missing.
  • It says nothing about Fortress, this project or its pipeline.
  • It advises leaving each agent's tier unset. Both designs set a tier on every agent because the brief told them to.

Choices that came from the brief, not from the designers

  • The tiers: Opus for every worker and checker, Fable only for rulings, Sonnet only for archaeology. The Opus design uses Sonnet for a cost measurement. The Fable design stretches Sonnet to the gate and the landing, and asks you first Fable §5.
  • Test first, the test committed alone, and checked by reading the worker's transcript.
  • The two full suites run once on the merged tree before landing.
  • One base build before the launch, every worktree seeded from it in about 3 s Brief, and the old code run from that base build.
  • Every long wait polled in steps under 5 minutes, because of the cache: 270 s in the Fable design Fable §2, 260 s in the Opus design Opus §1.
  • The longest rung started first, because only two agents run at a time.
  • A run stopped at 13 hours is resumed from its journal.

What is left as the designers' own: how many checkers, when a ruling happens and on which tier, and what runs after the rungs.

How blind they were: partly

  • Withheld: the pipeline script, its manual, the record's sections 6 to 8, the batch reviews and the post-mortems Brief.
  • But section 1 of the record ends with "Cost": batch 9's cost by stage (workers 2.69M, first skeptics 1.24M, two refusal chains 1.40M, the tail 1.56M) and the old pipeline's estimate for batch 10, 6M to 7M Rec §1. Both designs measure their savings against these numbers.
  • Section 1 also defines a rung, the skeptic and the gate. Section 4 names the gather and the order it merges in Rec §1, §4.
  • Section 3's rung texts carry lines of the existing pipeline: each rung's "For the skeptic" paragraph and its gate lines. The brief said so and asked the designers to read them as the old way Brief.
  • POSITIONS describes parts of it: the shared base build and a skeptic that reads instead of rebuilding ("Nothing is built or run twice on the same code."), the merged-diff review beside the gate ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), and Opus for a judge's first ruling, Fable for a second ("The judge's rulings.") POSITIONS.
  • explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, which the brief pointed to, describes batch 8's skeptics, second skeptics and second gate in its section 4.
  • The Opus designer declares a slip. The file viewer returned the record in two pages, and it read the second, sections 6 to 8. It marks what it took from them with [6-8]: the reuse of the base build, the briefings' sizes and the worker time guesses Opus header.

So both designers knew the pipeline's shape in part: worker, skeptic, one repair, merge, gate. The experiment shows best what each would change in that shape, not what each would invent from nothing.

3The pipeline batch 10 runs on

Nine roles, all Opus but a judge's second ruling. Batch 9 spent 6.88M on it B9 §7.

A rung's chain runs from its worker to its second skeptic. Everything after the rungs is called the tail. Tiers are set in Script :51–58. Each cost below is batch 9's measured spend B9 §7.

  1. Rung workerOpusone per rung

    Works in its own worktree (a copy of the tree on its own branch), seeded from the one base build. Writes the test, sees it fail, commits it alone, then makes the fix and its specification text, and pushes as it goes.

    Batch 9: 2.69M over 6 agents; about 2.2M without the VM restart B9 §7

  2. SkepticOpusone per rung

    Reads the worker's transcript to see the test failed first. Runs its own small programs on the new and the old code. Builds nothing. Approves or refuses. Since 3 Oct it refuses only when the fix needs code; a wording or record fix is a required correction that the gather makes Manual.

    Batch 9: 1.24M over 4 B9 §7

  3. JudgeOpusFable 2nd ruling

    Acts on a refusal, before any repair: it rules repair, drop or stop Script :2541–2552. A second ruling on the same rung runs on Fable.

    Batch 9: 0.45M over 2 B9 §7

  4. RepairOpus

    One round, in the rung's worktree, on the judge's ruling.

    Batch 9: 0.56M over 2 B9 §7

  5. Second skepticOpus

    Checks only the repair, against its own refusal.

    Batch 9: 0.40M over 2 B9 §7

  6. GatherOpus

    Puts each approved rung on main as one composed commit. Writes the ledger rows (the list of known defects), the FACTS and PLAN lines and the batch record.

    Batch 9: 0.47M B9 §7

  7. Merged-diff reviewOpus

    Runs beside the gate. Reads the merged diff and the records. A blocking finding in code gets its own judge and one repair.

    Batch 9: 0.42M, its judge 0.19M, its repair 0.20M B9 §7

  8. GateOpus

    Builds the merged tree once. Runs testFast, testSystem, the four-thread atomic runs, the compile ladder, and the two report-only stages: the checker count and the distance, two measures of what the compiled checker still refuses in the library Manual.

    Batch 9: 0.13M B9 §7

  9. CommitOpus

    Lands the gate's tables, pushes main, and starts the two microGPT runs under walk.

    Batch 9: 0.15M B9 §7

Batch 9, measured: 6.88M over 22 agents, 5 h 44 min. The tail: 1.56M B9 §7.

Batch 10 on this pipeline, the record's estimate: 6M to 7M, 14 to 18 agents, 6 to 9 hours Rec §1.

4The two designs

Both keep the shape: workers, a checker per rung or pair, one repair round, a merge, one gate. They differ in the checking and in the tail.

The Fable design

Before the launch the coordinator builds the base once, about 4 minutes, and puts each rung's section of the record into the run's arguments Fable §2. Order: C, W, N, G, two at a time Fable §1.

  1. WorkerOpus×4

    Its brief is its rung's section of the record, with no separate briefing. Tests first, committed alone. Then one suite run, chosen by what the edit can break: W runs testSystem; C runs the compiler and library tracks of testFast; G and N run only their own tests, which load the whole library. C, G and N run the two stages once at the end. It writes the ledger, FACTS and PLAN lines into its report, not into those files.

    Estimate: 2.5M to 3.3M Fable §4

  2. SkepticOpus×4

    Reads the git log, the diff, the report and the tool lines of the worker's transcript. Runs 3 to 6 programs of its own on new and old code. Builds nothing. It may refuse only on six listed grounds Fable §2:

    • a test not seen failing first, or not committed alone;
    • a stop of the brief met and not listed;
    • a fix against the text or library practice the brief cites;
    • a file touched outside the brief's list;
    • a value changed without the brief's warrant;
    • a test that cannot fail for the reason it names.

    Anything else is a note for you.

    Estimate: 0.8M to 1.2M, 0.2M to 0.3M each Fable §4

  3. After a refusalone chain expected
    • Opus Repair of exactly the named grounds: 0.3M.
    • Opus Second read, of those grounds only: 0.15M.
    • Opus Ruling, only if the second read refuses again, approve or drop: 0.15M.
    • Fable Second ruling, only if the Opus ruling says the dispute is a design question across two of the specification, the library and the implementation: 0.15M, rarely.

    A rung not approved stays on its branch; the batch lands without it.

    Estimate: 0.6M a chain; one expected, two budgeted Fable §4

  4. GatherOpus

    Merges the approved branches with merge commits in a seeded worktree, and writes the records from the workers' reports.

    Estimate: 0.25M Fable §4

  5. GateSonnet, low effort

    One build of the merged tree, then testFast, testSystem, the ladder, the count and the distance, one after another. A red gate gets one Opus repair and one more gate.

    Estimate: 0.10M to 0.15M; a red gate adds 0.4M and 0.1M, expected once in three batches Fable §4

  6. LandingSonnet, low effort

    Writes the gate's numbers into the landing note, fast-forwards main, pushes, starts the microGPT runs.

    Estimate: 0.08M Fable §4

Not in it: the merged-diff review, and a judge on every refusal Fable §1.

Estimate: about 5.2M (4.3M to 6.8M), including about 0.25M of the coordinator's own work outside the run. 11 to 19 agents, 13 to 14 expected. About 9 to 10 hours Fable §4.

The Opus design

Before the launch the coordinator builds or reuses the base build, renders each rung's briefing, and commits two small tools: gate.sh, the gate's steps as one script, and test-first-trace.py, which prints a worker's test runs from its transcript Opus §2, §5. Order: C, N, G, W, two at a time Opus §1.

  1. WorkerOpus×4

    Its rung's section plus its briefing. Tests first, committed alone; the fix; the text in the S1 form. One reach run, the part of the suite its change can reach: testFast for C, testSystem for W, N and G. C, N and G run the two stages once. New ledger rows get placeholders that the integrator numbers.

    Estimate: 2.25M (1.8M to 2.75M) Opus §4

  2. CheckerOpus×3

    One for W, one for C, and one for N and G together. Checks test first from git and the transcript, the paths touched, each fix against its text or precedent, at most eight programs of its own, the worker's results, and the revised text Opus §2. It may commit text-only corrections. It approves unless a code or test finding stands on a program or a cited line.

    Estimate: 0.88M (0.69M to 1.12M) Opus §4

  3. After a refusal1.4 expected
    • Opus Repair: accepts each finding, turning the checker's program into a test that fails first and then fixing it, or contests it with evidence. About 0.28M each, 0.43M expected.
    • Fable Ruling, only for a contested finding: one ruling, final. About 0.15M each, 0.05M expected.
    • Opus Second repair, only after an upheld ruling: 0.04M expected.

    No second skeptic.

    Estimates Opus §4

  4. IntegratorOpus

    Merges with merge commits into a fresh, unseeded worktree, numbers the rows, starts gate.sh in the background (a clean build and the full gate, 25 to 35 minutes Opus §2), and writes the records while it runs. Pushes a work branch, never main.

    Estimate: 0.28M Opus §4

  5. ReviewerOpusbeside the integrator

    Reads the four diffs side by side for what no single check could see. Its text corrections land before the push. Its code findings become rows for the next batch and block nothing.

    Estimate: 0.25M Opus §4

  6. Gate repairOpusred gate only

    Repairs the merged tree as a whole, then one more gate.

    Estimate: 0.1M expected (0.4M at a 0.25 chance) Opus §4

  7. LanderOpus, low effort

    Applies the review's text corrections, checks that no gated path changed since the gate, pushes main, starts the microGPT runs.

    Estimate: 0.08M Opus §4

  8. MeasureSonnet, low effort

    Measures the run's cost by role from its journal and writes it beside this estimate.

    Estimate: 0.1M Opus §4

Estimate: about 4.3M on Opus (3.0M to 6.4M), up to 0.2M on Fable, about 0.1M on Sonnet. 10 Opus agents and the measure in the base case, about 12 expected, 17 at worst. About 9.5 to 10 hours (8 to 12) Opus §4.

5Side by side, role by role

Both estimates are predictions, worked out by arithmetic from batch 9's figures. Neither is a measurement Fable §4 Opus §4.

Both put the largest part of their saving in the tail. Fable: the tail falls from 1.56M to about 0.5M, about 1.1M of its 1.7M below batch 9's 6.88M Fable §4. Opus: 0.8M of the 1.3M it assigns to stages comes from the tail; it puts its total saving at about 2M Opus §4.

6Where the tokens go today

A Sonnet measurement of batches 8 and 9 on the existing pipeline: 43 agents, 14.60M written Labor.

  • The fixed start. Every agent starts with 69K to 108K tokens of context before it does anything: the system prompt and tools, the harness's attachments, and its brief. Written across both batches, that is 2.84M, 19.5% of everything Labor. The 45K floor the designers were given Brief is the part before the brief, about 42K; today's briefs add 27K to 56K by role Labor.
  • Thinking. The agents' own thinking and narration is the largest single class: 3.92M, 26.9%. Whether it was all needed cannot be measured Labor.
  • Checking against building. Roles whose job is to check or judge hold 6.26M, 42.9% of the writes. Rung workers hold 36.7%. The refusal cycle (judge, repair, second skeptic) is 3.34M, 22.9%, because both batches refused two rungs Labor.
  • Exploring beyond the brief. Little, and mostly by searching. A rung worker reads 54K of its 536K (10%) beyond what its brief names. 74% of the files it opens beyond the brief are named in its briefing, FACTS or the maps. No agent opened INDEX.md Labor.
  • Reading a later agent repeats. 1.39M of 4.73M read (29%) were lines an earlier agent of the same batch had already been given. In a chain the followers repeat 750K of 1.77M (42%); the tail repeats 398K of 1.28M (31%). Much of this is the checking itself: an agent that does not look at the diff cannot check it. So 750K is a ceiling, not a saving Labor.

The eight levers, saving per batch

They overlap, and the measurement recommends none of them Labor.

  1. Let the cache share the identical start. 0.15M to 0.24M with today's 5-minute cache; 0.74M to 0.91M with a one-hour cache or a keep-warm call. Needs a harness feature; whether the Workflow tool offers one is unknown Labor.
  2. Several reads in one turn instead of one read a turn. 0.30M to 0.40M. Untested: it assumes the thinking between reads goes away Labor.
  3. The review fixes a text-only finding itself, without a judge and a repair. 0.3M to 0.35M when it recurs, as it did in both batches. Risk: in batch 9 the judge found two errors in the review's own proposed sentence Labor.
  4. The gate as a script, with an agent only on failure. 0.12M to 0.24M. A flaky stage or a failure still needs a model. The Opus design's gate.sh, started by the integrator, takes this route Labor Opus §2.
  5. Chain followers read only the briefing the worker had not. 0.07M to 0.12M. Weakens the skeptic's independent check against the record Labor.
  6. A shorter shared prefix for roles that do not need the worker's rules. 0.03M to 0.06M. Works against lever 1, which wants one identical block Labor.
  7. The gather leaves the review a digest. At most 0.07M. The high-risk lever: the review exists to check the gather Labor.
  8. File and line anchors in the brief for the searches. All search is up to 0.36M; if a fifth of it goes, 0.07M. The anchors go stale after the first edit Labor.

7Decisions put to you

Both designs' lists, merged. Each line names the design that raised it.

  • FableOpus The merged-diff review. Fable drops it; keeping it costs about 0.25M Fable §5. Opus keeps it beside the gate but never blocking; a blocking form adds about 0.3M Opus §5.
  • Opus One Fable ruling for a contested finding, in place of an Opus first ruling and a Fable second. About 0.05M of Fable a batch Opus §5.
  • Fable Approvals with required corrections. A skeptic writes a small fix into its verdict and the gather applies it, instead of a repair chain: about 0.6M down to about 50K when the fix is small Fable §5. The design runs the full round until you say yes.
  • Fable Sonnet runs the gate and the landing. About 0.1M less than Opus Fable §5.
  • Fable The gate builds the seeded merged tree, not a clean one. A clean build costs about 4 minutes more Fable §5. The Opus design builds clean without asking.
  • Fable Whether G and N may skip their own stage runs, their result then read from the gate's per-site list by section. The design runs them until you say Fable §5.
  • Opus testSystem run by each library rung, which their briefs leave to the gate. About 3 minutes and 10K each Opus §5. The Fable design runs no suite there.
  • Opus Merge commits on main, keeping the workers' test-then-fix commits, in place of one composed commit per rung. The Fable design merges the same way without asking.
  • Fable Launch details: rung W's P1 line and the ledger's first free row. The Opus design takes P1 as unanswered from the boot note.

Each design also lists what to measure before a run. Both ask that the top tier's name in the script be checked, and that reading test first from a worker's transcript be tried once before relying on it Fable §5 Opus §5.

8What comes next

  • Done: the measurement of where each role's tokens go, labor.md, section 6 above Labor.
  • Waiting on batch 10: its measured cost, once it lands.
  • Then: a Fable comparison of both designs with batch 10 as run, its measured cost and the token measurement Held.
  • After that: the same two designers at the whole project's scope Held.

lines: ## Boot note to the resumed coordinator

-**What is in flight, for the coordinator after a compaction; rewritten whole at every change, never appended.** Written at 07:45 UTC on 2026-10-03. When Pavol reads turn by turn: acknowledge each new point in a line and put it on the held list below with the UTC time of his message; do not tack "holding" onto full answers. The coordinating session runs on Opus, Fable kept for judgements and reviews (POSITIONS, "Which tier runs what."). **Pavol is awake.** His panel at about 04:50 UTC: all models 31% used, Fable 9%, both reset Friday 12:00 his time (10:00 UTC). **Running: climb batch 10**, run `wf_d5ec6194-bcc`, launched 05:27 UTC on his word ("we should run batch 10") and the standing go, base `9c9e823d56144771e4dcc1ee75de1f13132898b1` (the splice commit, LEDGER_FROM 610), `baseBuild` `/home/user/fortress-base10` (at `cec70988b`, code identical, scoped status clean, a trial seed 3 s), rungs W `rung-walk-meet` (without P1's half), C `rung-checker-defects`, G `rung-generator-slips`, N `rung-number-order-slips`, scatter C, N, G, W; the record `CLIMB-BATCH-10.md` reviewed by Fable in place (`e2a7838fc`, `climb-batch-10-review.md`, no question for Pavol); about 6M expected. +description: A probe of prompt caching across workflow agents; answers one line and reads nothing.
+model: opus

+You are a cache probe in an experiment on prompt caching. Do not use any tool. Answer the task in one line. The reference text below is only there to make this system prompt large; do not summarise it.
+## Execution model
+- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).

+- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.

+- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).

+- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).

+- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost, 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` in Java models of the program's three kernels, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles: the compiler prelude lacks the array types, with `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305, wider than row 72). On the interpreter, the only path that runs the kernels, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch and 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). The two one-line runtime defects the probe found are fixed (rows 302, 303; the next two entries), and no array type goes into the compiler prelude: the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (POSITIONS, the library route). A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`).

+- The boxing probe's scalar-loop reading, 156× primitive Java with boxing about 2% of it, is of the tree before rung 0's two fixes (rows 302, 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`); of the costs it named, `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7%) and the representational rest (about 30%) are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).

+- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).

+- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).

+- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine: the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s in another session, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).

+- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes.

+- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).

You remember it right, and it's on record: the batch design of 09-17, corrected on 09-18 and measured then.

- **What was measured:** four agents with one identical opening block in their prompts.
  - Agent 0 wrote about 44K and read nothing.
  - Agents 1 to 3 each read only about 33K from the cache: the system prompt and tools.
  - Each wrote its own prompt again, about 11K, even though most of that text was identical.
- **Why:** the cache can only be read at fixed cut points the harness places, after the system prompt and at the end of a message. A shared opening inside one message, with a different ending, is not such a point. So only a whole identical message hits, and our prompts never are, since each carries its rung's tail. That's your takeaway.
- **New since then:** this morning's measurement found even the system-prompt part is read from cache by only 19 of 43 agents. The cache lives 5 minutes, and agents start further apart than that.

**The workaround I'm testing now,** a small workflow of six one-line agents, a few hundred K at most:
- **The idea:** move the shared block into a custom agent type's own system prompt, which ends at one of those cut points. Every agent of that type should then read it from the cache.
- **The probe:** three agents of such a type, then three ordinary agents as a control. Two of the control agents get identical prompts and one a different last line.
- **If the custom type works,** the next step is a keep-warm agent of the same type that pings every 4 minutes, so the block stays cached across the hours a batch runs.

I'll report the numbers when it's done.

content.text:
I re-measured it, and your takeaway holds exactly. Three agents, one run:
- **Identical prompt:** the second agent read all 62K from the cache and wrote nothing.
- **Same prompt, only the last line different:** the third read just the system prompt and tools (35K) and wrote its whole 27K message again.

So only a whole identical message gets a cache hit, and each of our agents carries its own rung's part.

**The workaround test is blocked until this afternoon:**
- The idea is to put the shared block into a custom agent type's own system prompt, which ends at a cut point the cache can use.
- I wrote that agent type, but the harness only reads agent types when the session's process starts. So it can't be used until the platform's restart at about 12:33 UTC.
- I've set the 12:40 check-in to run that probe.
- If it works, the next step is a keep-warm agent of the same type, so the block stays cached across a whole batch.

**The fallback idea:**
- Give every agent the same identical prompt.
- Have each fetch its own rung's part as its first tool call, from a small script that hands out the next unclaimed brief.

**What it's worth:** this morning's measurement puts it at 0.15M to 0.24M a batch with today's 5-minute cache, and up to about 0.9M if the shared start can be kept warm. That's 2% to 13% of a batch, so worth the test, but not the largest lever.

content.text:
**How batch content is chosen.**
- **The one measure:** phase 3 has a single measure, the distance: the errors the compiled checker still reports on the one library, 340 after batch 9. The phase ends at zero.
- **The source:** each landing's gate writes the full list of those errors, each with its place and its class.
- **The planner** (an Opus worker) sorts that list into three piles:
  1. **Decided and free to fix:** one-off library slips, and checker defects with a known fix. These go into the batch.
  2. **Waiting on your decision or a judgement.** These are held and listed:
     - the arrays, 98 errors, after the switch-over by your answer
     - the self-typed bodies, 30, which need a list of ways and a judgement first
     - `isLeftZero`, which is yours to decide
  3. **Waiting on a probe:** P1's half. Probed first.
- **Added to pile 1:**
  - defects the last batch's review routed as owed: walk's rows 544, 534, 588
  - items PLAN queued: the checker rung after batch 8
  - your decisions ready to build: item 20
- **Grouping:** by code area, so that no two rungs touch the same declaration. Usually four rungs, because one landing pays for all of them and only two agents run at once.
- **Then:** Fable reviews the record, and you are asked only if a pile-2 item needs your word.
- **What's not a rule:** no target size per batch and no target cost per error. The planner takes whatever from pile 1 fits into four non-overlapping rungs.
- **Batch 10 by this rule:** 148 of the 340 errors in pile 1, 192 held.

**The rerun:** yes, I think it's worth it. The first run leaked so much that it measured our pipeline trimmed down, not a design from scratch. To do it clean:
- **A content-only brief first:** a Sonnet worker writes, for each piece of work, the defect, the files and lines, the decisions that bind it, and what done means (which tests pass, which rows close). No pipeline words (skeptic, gate, judge, rung), and no costs of past batches.
- **Your requirements cut to the minimum:**
  - test first, the test kept
  - suites green before anything reaches `main`
  - nothing built twice
  - only what `main` should hold gets committed
  - the specification revised with each change
- **No tier rule this time:** they get the prices and pools of Opus, Sonnet and Fable and choose for themselves. That answers your earlier question of what the `workflow-authoring` reference does on its own.
- **Machine facts as a short list** inside the brief: 4 CPUs, two agents at a time, the 5-minute cache, build and suite times, a built tree copied in 3 seconds.
- **What they may read:** that brief, the code, the specification and the ledger, and nothing under `explorations/coordinator` or the reviews.
- **Cost:** about 0.2M for the brief, 0.4M for Opus and 0.5M for Fable, about 1.1M in all.

**Q: Run the blind rerun?**
1. **Yes, as above,** about 1.1M. The page then shows the leaky and the clean designs side by side.
2. **No.** Wait for the whole-project designs, which would need the same blinding anyway.

Recommendation: 1.

+# The process-engineering study
+## The question

+Pavol, 2026-10-03, early morning UTC: whether the way the work is run spends the weekly token pool well, and how to divide the pool between improving the process and moving the climb forward. His threads, in his order:

+- Why sharing the build between worktrees was called impossible for two weeks, and whether a model given the goal finds the answer ("machine empathy": "this empathy for machine, not wasting resources, is a crucial component of good engineering taste"; "Three seconds versus 0.07 ... if it's better, then let's use it").

+- Where each role's tokens go inside a batch, and what is shared between agents that could be done once ("I am perfectly aware that checking and rechecking is the necessary part ... I just want to understand whether that's it").

+- Whether one fixed batch workflow, reused for every step of the climb, holds the project back against what a designer would build from the goals alone ("I want to see those designs for the ultra code workflows, but not run them").
+- Whether the identical start of every agent can be read from the prompt cache.
+## Done

+- `cache-sharing.md`: why cache sharing was called impossible (an Opus 5 review's measured "file names differ" written as "cannot be given a warm cache at all", carried by every tier after), the blinded test on both tiers (both found the translation in about 15 minutes given the goal), and the rebuilds priced (245 of 425 builds avoidable over 18 batch runs, about 7.3 hours of agent time, 0.87M tokens: the waste was time, not tokens).

+- `p1-cost.md`: how probe P1 wrote 7.0M against a stated 0.5M (19 context rewrites after ten-minute waits its brief did not cap; never put to Pavol). His rule from it: POSITIONS, "The coordinator watches what it launches." (long runs only).

+- The blinded engineers' improvements built (`5b0a82d97`; `coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md` section 6): seeded worktrees take the base's file dates (a Java edit's rebuild 143 s to 77 s, and a defect fixed: a branch whose Java differed from the base was never recompiled), and `tools/old-fortress.sh` runs the old code from the base build with a private cache folder (0.04 s, 36 MB, against a 3 s, 206 MB copy per rung). The script and manual change waits for batch 10's landing: the replacement texts are in the coordinator's scratchpad, `old-fortress-script-patch.md`, and the boot note names it.

+- `labor.md`: where the tokens of batches 8 and 9 went (14.6M): the fixed start of every agent 19.5%, the agents' own thinking 27%, checking roles 43% against rung workers 37%, exploration beyond the brief about 10% of a worker, 29% of what agents read already given to an earlier agent of the batch; eight levers, together about 1M to 1.5M a batch.

+- The first designs for batch 10's goals, `design-batch10-fable.md` (about 5.2M) and `design-batch10-opus.md` (about 4.3M on Opus), from `design-batch10-brief.md`. They are not blind: the record's section 1 carried batch 9's cost by stage, its section 3 lines of the pipeline, POSITIONS and the build-cache note parts of it, and the Opus designer read the record's sections 6 to 8 by a paging slip. # The machine and its prices

Facts about this container and the tools on it, with numbers. They were checked against `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` (its test-harness and container sections), the files it cites, `explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`, the header lines of the two measurement scripts and the last full run's summary. Times are wall-clock seconds on this machine; a run beside other work is slow

## The machine

- **CPUs: 4** (Intel Xeon at 2.8 GHz, `nproc` = 4); about 15 GB of memory (`free -g`, measured now). OpenJDK 25. The suites pin one interpreter thread per JVM (`FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, set in `build.xml`), so the four cores are used by running several JVMs at once (`ant testFast` runs four tracks that occupy the four cores; `ant testSystem` is split into four shards).
- **Heaps.** `bin/fortress` gives its JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set; the `ant testSystem` harness 768 MB; `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, which every measurement script expects to be sourced, sets 4 GB.
- **Disk.** Every run that imports a grammar writes a 5.8 MB parser directory to `/tmp` (`/tmp/fortress<random>rats`) and never deletes it; 723 of them (4.2 GB) once filled the disk allowance and broke a tool's output with "no space left on device". Sourcing `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them; check `df` before a long run.
- **Build commands.** `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`, `export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH`, `export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>`, `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, then `ant compileAll` from the repository root. `ant compileAll` deletes the whole `default_repository/caches` including the tracked file `default_repository/caches/global.map`: restore it with `git checkout -- default_repos

## The times

- `ant compileAll`: 57 s in the last full run; 82 s on a fresh checkout; 25 to 40 s on an already built tree after a small edit.
- The library compile (the five components in order, after `ant compileAll`): 108 to 112 s (AnyType 17, CompilerBuiltin 63, CompilerLibrary 27, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 2); one component alone 2 to 63 s. A base built from nothing, `ant compileAll` plus the library compile plus one walk run, is about 200 s.
- `ant testFast`: 635 s (10 min 35 s) in the last full run, 1,782 tests, 0 failures; the longest single suite in it takes about 440 s, so more parallelism does not shorten it much.
- `ant testSystem`: 243 s (4 min 3 s) in the last full run, 504 tests in four shards, 0 failures.
- The checker-count measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]`; it counts the errors the compiled checker reports on the library before each api's early return, 1 now): about 20 s alone on an idle machine when first measured (the library has grown since); 139 s when it ran beside other jobs.
- The distance measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]`; it runs every phase of the compiled checker over all twelve apis and twelve components in one JVM on one busy core and counts every distinct error, 340 now): 1,212 s (20 min) in the last full run, 732 s of it on `FortressLibrary` alone; 789 s on an idle machine earlier; 14 to 24 minutes
- One walk run of a small program: about 8 s on cold caches. A compile of a small program: about 5 s, its run about 1 s.

## Copying a build, and running the old code

- **A built tree can be copied into a new worktree in about 3 s**: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]`. The base worktree must have been built once (`ant compileAll`, the restore of `global.map`, the library compile). The copy (206 MB: build 40 MB, caches 36 MB) runs walk and the compiled path without building anything, and its 
- **The base's code runs beside the new code** with a private cache folder: `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...` (for example `old-fortress.sh <base-build> <dir>/old-caches compile P.fss`, then `... run P`, or `... P.fss` for walk). The private folder is a copy of the base's caches, 36 MB made in 0.04 s; the run writes nothing that 

## The agents and their prices

- **How many agents run at once: 2.** The multi-agent harness (the script-driven tool that starts agents in parallel or in sequence) runs two agents at a time on this box; more wait for a free slot.
- **An agent's floor is about 45,000 tokens before it does anything** (system prompt, tools, first message). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (about 33,000 tokens read) and not the first user message (about 11,000 tokens written by each agent). Agents started with an identical whole prompt share the cache (the second reads what the first wrote and write
- **The prompt cache lives 1 hour for the main session and 5 minutes for a subagent.** A call within the life reads the cache and renews it, so a wait taken in steps shorter than the life costs a cache read per step. A wait longer than the life makes the next call write the agent's whole context again with no cache read: a subagent holding a 250,000-token context that waits 8 minutes on a build wr
- **The Bash tool's time limit is 10 minutes** (600 s) for a foreground call (default 2 minutes); the call is killed at the limit. A longer command runs in the background and is polled.
- **The project counts cost as tokens written**: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.
- **Three model tiers are available: Opus, Sonnet and Fable.** Fable is the strongest and draws on a separate, scarcer weekly pool; Sonnet is the cheapest. An agent that names no model inherits the session's.
- **An agent call can come back empty.** The harness returns null for an agent it has marked failed, even when the agent delivered its structured result first (the platform's safety filter has ended agents this way); a design must expect it.
- **The platform stops the session's process after about 13 hours** (12 h 58 min of continuous running; the stops fall at 46,636 to 46,660 s) and restarts it in resume mode within seconds. The restart kills every running harness run and every running agent; the conversation, the worktrees, the transcripts and each run's journal survive. **A run of the harness is resumed from its journal**: agents 
=====
## 1. Terms and facts the pieces rely on

- **Walk** is the interpreter: `./bin/fortress file.fss` (the file name without `.fss` must equal the component name). Its load-time checks run when a component is loaded, before `run()`. **The compiled path** is `fortress compile` then `fortress run`; its static type checker, **the checker**, also runs over the library. Both paths must keep working.
- **The one library** is the interpreter's library, `Library/*.fsi` (the apis) and `Library/*.fss` (the components) together with `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/` (`FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray`, `AnyType`, and so on): `FortressLibrary`, `List`, `String`, `FlatString`, `Stream`, `Writer`, `RangeInternals`, `NatReflect`, `TypeProxy`, `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray`, `AnyType`. It is to become the library that the compiler checks. The compiler's own smaller prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `Compile
- **The ledger** is `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`: a table of every known gap, one row each, the row number in the first column. "Row 544" means that row. A row has a status (for example NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, FIXED), the specification passage that settles it and a note.
- **The specification** is `Specification/` (LaTeX). **Appendix I** is `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, the revival's list of changes, one subsection per entry. `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched. The **S1 form** (decision "S1 form", section 4) is how every change to the text is written.
- **Test corpora.** `ProjectFortress/tests/` holds the interpreter tests (run under walk by `ant testSystem`); `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `ProjectFortress/library_tests/` hold the compiled-path tests (run by `ant testFast`, which also runs the unit tests of the compiler). A `.test` file beside a program holds its keys (`compile`, `link`, `run`, `compile_err_contains=...`, `run_out_contains=...`, `load_exception_contains=...`, `tests=` the component name). A test file named `XXX...` is
- **What a test can hold.** In `tests/` a program that walk must refuse at load is held by `load_exception_contains=<text>` (the test passes when the load fails with that text; as an `XXX` file it is the expected failure that walk loads and runs instead). In `compiler_tests/` an `XXX` test can express a compile-time failure only: a defect that compiles but misbehaves at run time needs two `.test` files over one component (a plain-named one driving `link`, an `XXX`-named one driving `run` with a 
- **The interpreter suite is split in four.** `ant testSystem` runs four shards of `tests/`, each file kept by its index in the sorted list modulo 4; a file added moves every later file along the shards, so only the sum of the four shards' test counts is comparable across a change to `tests/`.
- **The distance measurement's class codes** (section 5) name kinds of error. The ones the pieces use: OT other one-off library slips and checker limits; NM names the api does not declare; D1 an abstract method that is a bodyless function under compiled desugaring; MB `Just` and `Nothing` do not join to `Maybe`; BR a big operator's body typed as the element, not the `BigReduction` or `Comprehension` declared; I2 and I3 integers in generic code (I2 the dummy-`ZZ32` device of `#` and `:`; I3 a num
- **A caution on reading the measurement.** The distance measurement's class table sorts errors by fixed library line ranges, so an edit that inserts lines in a library file misfiles errors by class (ledger row 577). The per-site list of the measurement (each error's location and message) is the reliable reading, with its lines mapped through the edit's diff.

The suites pin one interpreter thread per JVM (`FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, set in `build.xml`), so the four cores are used by running several JVMs at once (`ant testFast` runs four tracks that occupy the four cores; `ant testSystem` is split into four shards).
- **Heaps.** `bin/fortress` gives its JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set; the `ant testSystem` harness 768 MB; `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, which every measurement script expects to be sourced, sets 4 GB.
- **Disk.** Every run that imports a grammar writes a 5.8 MB parser directory to `/tmp` (`/tmp/fortress<random>rats`) and never deletes it; 723 of them (4.2 GB) once filled the disk allowance and broke a tool's output with "no space left on device". Sourcing `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them; check `df` before a long run.
- **Build commands.** `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`, `export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH`, `export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>`, `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, then `ant compileAll` from the repository root. `ant compileAll` deletes the whole `default_repository/caches` including the tracked file `default_repository/caches/global.map`: restore it with `git checkout -- default_repos

## The times

- `ant compileAll`: 57 s in the last full run; 82 s on a fresh checkout; 25 to 40 s on an already built tree after a small edit.
- The library compile (the five components in order, after `ant compileAll`): 108 to 112 s (AnyType 17, CompilerBuiltin 63, CompilerLibrary 27, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 2); one component alone 2 to 63 s. A base built from nothing, `ant compileAll` plus the library compile plus one walk run, is about 200 s.
- `ant testFast`: 635 s (10 min 35 s) in the last full run, 1,782 tests, 0 failures; the longest single suite in it takes about 440 s, so more parallelism does not shorten it much.
- `ant testSystem`: 243 s (4 min 3 s) in the last full run, 504 tests in four shards, 0 failures.
- The checker-count measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]`; it counts the errors the compiled checker reports on the library before each api's early return, 1 now): about 20 s alone on an idle machine when first measured (the library has grown since); 139 s when it ran beside other jobs.
- The distance measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]`; it runs every phase of the compiled checker over all twelve apis and twelve components in one JVM on one busy core and counts every distinct error, 340 now): 1,212 s (20 min) in the last full run, 732 s of it on `FortressLibrary` alone; 789 s on an idle machine earlier; 14 to 24 minutes
- One walk run of a small program: about 8 s on cold caches. A compile of a small program: about 5 s, its run about 1 s.

## Copying a build, and running the old code

- **A built tree can be copied into a new worktree in about 3 s**: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]`. The base worktree must have been built once (`ant compileAll`, the restore of `global.map`, the library compile). The copy (206 MB: build 40 MB, caches 36 MB) runs walk and the compiled path without building anything, and its 
- **The base's code runs beside the new code** with a private cache folder: `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...` (for example `old-fortress.sh <base-build> <dir>/old-caches compile P.fss`, then `... run P`, or `... P.fss` for walk). The private folder is a copy of the base's caches, 36 MB made in 0.04 s; the run writes nothing that 

## The agents and their prices

- **How many agents run at once: 2.** The multi-agent harness (the script-driven tool that starts agents in parallel or in sequence) runs two agents at a time on this box; more wait for a free slot.
- **An agent's floor is about 45,000 tokens before it does anything** (system prompt, tools, first message). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (about 33,000 tokens read) and not the first user message (about 11,000 tokens written by each agent). Agents started with an identical whole prompt share the cache (the second reads what the first wrote and write
- **The prompt cache lives 1 hour for the main session and 5 minutes for a subagent.** A call within the life reads the cache and renews it, so a wait taken in steps shorter than the life costs a cache read per step. A wait longer than the life makes the next call write the agent's whole context again with no cache read: a subagent holding a 250,000-token context that waits 8 minutes on a build wr
- **The Bash tool's time limit is 10 minutes** (600 s) for a foreground call (default 2 minutes); the call is killed at the limit. A longer command runs in the background and is polled.
- **The project counts cost as tokens written**: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.
- **Three model tiers are available: Opus, Sonnet and Fable.** Fable is the strongest and draws on a separate, scarcer weekly pool; Sonnet is the cheapest. An agent that names no model inherits the session's.
- **An agent call can come back empty.** The harness returns null for an agent it has marked failed, even when the agent delivered its structured result first (the platform's safety filter has ended agents this way); a design must expect it.
- **The platform stops the session's process after about 13 hours** (12 h 58 min of continuous running; the stops fall at 46,636 to 46,660 s) and restarts it in resume mode within seconds. The restart kills every running harness run and every running agent; the conversation, the worktrees, the transcripts and each run's journal survive. **A run of the harness is resumed from its journal**: agents 
=====
## 1. Terms and facts the pieces rely on

- **Walk** is the interpreter: `./bin/fortress file.fss` (the file name without `.fss` must equal the component name). Its load-time checks run when a component is loaded, before `run()`. **The compiled path** is `fortress compile` then `fortress run`; its static type checker, **the checker**, also runs over the library. Both paths must keep working.
- **The one library** is the interpreter's library, `Library/*.fsi` (the apis) and `Library/*.fss` (the components) together with `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/` (`FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray`, `AnyType`, and so on): `FortressLibrary`, `List`, `String`, `FlatString`, `Stream`, `Writer`, `RangeInternals`, `NatReflect`, `TypeProxy`, `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray`, `AnyType`. It is to become the library that the compiler checks. The compiler's own smaller prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `Compile
- **The ledger** is `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`: a table of every known gap, one row each, the row number in the first column. "Row 544" means that row. A row has a status (for example NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, FIXED), the specification passage that settles it and a note.
- **The specification** is `Specification/` (LaTeX). **Appendix I** is `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, the revival's list of changes, one subsection per entry. `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched. The **S1 form** (decision "S1 form", section 4) is how every change to the text is written.
- **Test corpora.** `ProjectFortress/tests/` holds the interpreter tests (run under walk by `ant testSystem`); `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `ProjectFortress/library_tests/` hold the compiled-path tests (run by `ant testFast`, which also runs the unit tests of the compiler). A `.test` file beside a program holds its keys (`compile`, `link`, `run`, `compile_err_contains=...`, `run_out_contains=...`, `load_exception_contains=...`, `tests=` the component name). A test file named `XXX...` is
- **What a test can hold.** In `tests/` a program that walk must refuse at load is held by `load_exception_contains=<text>` (the test passes when the load fails with that text; as an `XXX` file it is the expected failure that walk loads and runs instead). In `compiler_tests/` an `XXX` test can express a compile-time failure only: a defect that compiles but misbehaves at run time needs two `.test` files over one component (a plain-named one driving `link`, an `XXX`-named one driving `run` with a 
- **The interpreter suite is split in four.** `ant testSystem` runs four shards of `tests/`, each file kept by its index in the sorted list modulo 4; a file added moves every later file along the shards, so only the sum of the four shards' test counts is comparable across a change to `tests/`.
- **The distance measurement's class codes** (section 5) name kinds of error. The ones the pieces use: OT other one-off library slips and checker limits; NM names the api does not declare; D1 an abstract method that is a bodyless function under compiled desugaring; MB `Just` and `Nothing` do not join to `Maybe`; BR a big operator's body typed as the element, not the `BigReduction` or `Comprehension` declared; I2 and I3 integers in generic code (I2 the dummy-`ZZ32` device of `#` and `:`; I3 a num
- **A caution on reading the measurement.** The distance measurement's class table sorts errors by fixed library line ranges, so an edit that inserts lines in a library file misfiles errors by class (ledger row 577). The per-site list of the measurement (each error's location and message) is the reliable reading, with its lines mapped through the edit's diff.

**This is a design experiment. Do not run anything:** no Workflow, no Agent, no ant, no build, no Fortress run, no test. Read, think and write one document.

  - Fable implements the three hardest edits, the ones that restate a rule every test passes through.

- **It flags the same tension I did:** for the library repairs, no test can fail before the change until the switch-over, so rule 1 needs your reading there.

The Opus design is still running. I'll compare the two once it lands.

lines: +# The machine and its prices

+Facts about this container and the tools on it, with numbers. They were checked against `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` (its test-harness and container sections), the files it cites, `explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`, the header lines of the two measurement scripts and the last full run's summary. Times are wall-clock seconds on this machine; a run beside other work is slower.
+## The machine

+- **CPUs: 4** (Intel Xeon at 2.8 GHz, `nproc` = 4); about 15 GB of memory (`free -g`, measured now). OpenJDK 25. The suites pin one interpreter thread per JVM (`FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, set in `build.xml`), so the four cores are used by running several JVMs at once (`ant testFast` runs four tracks that occupy the four cores; `ant testSystem` is split into four shards).

+- **Heaps.** `bin/fortress` gives its JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set; the `ant testSystem` harness 768 MB; `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, which every measurement script expects to be sourced, sets 4 GB.

+- **Disk.** Every run that imports a grammar writes a 5.8 MB parser directory to `/tmp` (`/tmp/fortress<random>rats`) and never deletes it; 723 of them (4.2 GB) once filled the disk allowance and broke a tool's output with "no space left on device". Sourcing `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them; check `df` before a long run.

+- **Build commands.** `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`, `export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH`, `export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>`, `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, then `ant compileAll` from the repository root. `ant compileAll` deletes the whole `default_repository/caches` including the tracked file `default_repository/caches/global.map`: restore it with `git checkout -- default_repository/caches/global.map` after every `ant compileAll`, and never commit its deletion. A compiled run (`fortress compile`, `fortress run`) needs the library compiled in order after a rebuild (AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary, CompilerAlgebra, CompilerSystem); stale caches give a misleading `NoSuchMethodError`. Walk does not need that order; its first run warms its own caches.
+## The times
+- `ant compileAll`: 57 s in the last full run; 82 s on a fresh checkout; 25 to 40 s on an already built tree after a small edit.

+- The library compile (the five components in order, after `ant compileAll`): 108 to 112 s (AnyType 17, CompilerBuiltin 63, CompilerLibrary 27, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 2); one component alone 2 to 63 s. A base built from nothing, `ant compileAll` plus the library compile plus one walk run, is about 200 s.
+- `ant testFast`: 635 s (10 min 35 s) in the last full run, 1,782 tests, 0 failures; the longest single suite in it takes about 440 s, so more parallelism does not shorten it much.
+- `ant testSystem`: 243 s (4 min 3 s) in the last full run, 504 tests in four shards, 0 failures.

+- The checker-count measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]`; it counts the errors the compiled checker reports on the library before each api's early return, 1 now): about 20 s alone on an idle machine when first measured (the library has grown since); 139 s when it ran beside other jobs.

+- The distance measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]`; it runs every phase of the compiled checker over all twelve apis and twelve components in one JVM on one busy core and counts every distinct error, 340 now): 1,212 s (20 min) in the last full run, 732 s of it on `FortressLibrary` alone; 789 s on an idle machine earlier; 14 to 24 minutes under load.
+- One walk run of a small program: about 8 s on cold caches. A compile of a small program: about 5 s, its run about 1 s.
+## Copying a build, and running the old code

+- **A built tree can be copied into a new worktree in about 3 s**: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]`. The base worktree must have been built once (`ant compileAll`, the restore of `global.map`, the library compile). The copy (206 MB: build 40 MB, caches 36 MB) runs walk and the compiled path without building anything, and its paths are translated for the new location.

+- **The base's code runs beside the new code** with a private cache folder: `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...` (for example `old-fortress.sh <base-build> <dir>/old-caches compile P.fss`, then `... run P`, or `... P.fss` for walk). The private folder is a copy of the base's caches, 36 MB made in 0.04 s; the run writes nothing that stays in the base build. Keep the private folder and the programs outside the base build.
+## The agents and their prices
+- **How many agents run at once: 2.** The multi-agent harness (the script-driven tool that starts agents in parallel or in sequence) runs two agents at a time on this box; more wait for a free slot.

+- **An agent's floor is about 45,000 tokens before it does anything** (system prompt, tools, first message). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (about 33,000 tokens read) and not the first user message (about 11,000 tokens written by each agent). Agents started with an identical whole prompt share the cache (the second reads what the first wrote and writes nothing); a prompt that differs only in its last line shares only the system prompt and tools (about 35,000 tokens read) and writes the rest again.

+- **The prompt cache lives 1 hour for the main session and 5 minutes for a subagent.** A call within the life reads the cache and renews it, so a wait taken in steps shorter than the life costs a cache read per step. A wait longer than the life makes the next call write the agent's whole context again with no cache read: a subagent holding a 250,000-token context that waits 8 minutes on a build writes 250,000 tokens at its next call.
+- **The Bash tool's time limit is 10 minutes** (600 s) for a foreground call (default 2 minutes); the call is killed at the limit. A longer command runs in the background and is polled.
+- **The project counts cost as tokens written**: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.

+- **Three model tiers are available: Opus, Sonnet and Fable.** Fable is the strongest and draws on a separate, scarcer weekly pool; Sonnet is the cheapest. An agent that names no model inherits the session's.

+- **An agent call can come back empty.** The harness returns null for an agent it has marked failed, even when the agent delivered its structured result first (the platform's safety filter has ended agents this way); a design must expect it.

+- **The platform stops the session's process after about 13 hours** (12 h 58 min of continuous running; the stops fall at 46,636 to 46,660 s) and restarts it in resume mode within seconds. content.text:
Opus's blind design is in too (`process-engineering/design-batch10-blind-opus.md`). It is the leanest of the four.

- **Shape:** six implementers, with the checker piece split three ways by file.
  - A run log records every code state already built or run, so nothing is repeated.
  - Reviewers try to refute each change while the merged builds and suites run in the background.
  - A fix happens only where something was found, then one gate and one squashed commit.
- **Tiers, its own choice:** Fable for the hardest checker piece only, Opus for implementers and reviewers, Sonnet for every launch, collection, gate and landing.
- **Its own estimate:** about 18 agents, 3.3M, 8.6 hours. Compare batch 9's measured 6.9M and the blind Fable design's 7.1M.

**Both blind designers raised your rule 1 for the library repairs:** no test can fail before such a fix until the switch-over. The record already answers this, so it's not a new question for you. Such a piece's test is the distance measurement, and its "before" is the last gate's tables (POSITIONS, "No re-measuring what the record holds."). The blind brief left that out with the pipeline words.

**Two real risks for batch 10 that Opus spotted while reading** (passed to the post-batch review):
- Row 604's compiled test needs `ImmutableArray`, which the compiler's prelude doesn't declare.
- W's new load check has the same shape as `String`'s `||` family of operators, which must keep loading. W's own interpreter suite run should show it either way.

The page is being extended with the blind rerun. I'll send the updated link when it's republished.

# The process-engineering study

## The question

Pavol, 2026-10-03, early morning UTC: whether the way the work is run spends the weekly token pool well, and how to divide the pool between improving the process and moving the climb forward. His threads, in his order:

- Why sharing the build between worktrees was called impossible for two weeks, and whether a model given the goal finds the answer ("machine empathy": "this empathy for machine, not wasting resources, is a crucial component of good engineering taste"; "Three seconds versus 0.07 ... if it's better, then let's use it").
- Where each role's tokens go inside a batch, and what is shared between agents that could be done once ("I am perfectly aware that checking and rechecking is the necessary part ... I just want to understand whether that's it").
- Whether one fixed batch workflow, reused for every step of the climb, holds the project back against what a designer would build from the goals alone ("I want to see those designs for the ultra code workflows, but not run them").
- Whether the identical start of every agent can be read from the prompt cache.

## Done

- `cache-sharing.md`: why cache sharing was called impossible (an Opus 5 review's measured "file names differ" written as "cannot be given a warm cache at all", carried by every tier after), the blinded test on both tiers (both found the translation in about 15 minutes given the goal), and the rebuilds priced (245 of 425 builds avoidable over 18 batch runs, about 7.3 hours of agent time, 0.87M tokens: the waste was time, not tokens).
- `p1-cost.md`: how probe P1 wrote 7.0M against a stated 0.5M (19 context rewrites after ten-minute waits its brief did not cap; never put to Pavol). His rule from it: POSITIONS, "The coordinator watches what it launches." (long runs only).
- The blinded engineers' improvements built (`5b0a82d97`; `coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md` section 6): seeded worktrees take the base's file dates (a Java edit's rebuild 143 s to 77 s, and a defect fixed: a branch whose Java differed from the base was never recompiled), and `tools/old-fortress.sh` runs the old code from the base build with a private cache folder (0.04 s, 36 MB, against a 3 s, 206 MB copy per rung). The script and manual change waits for batch 10's landing: the replacement texts are in the coordinator's scratchpad, `old-fortress-script-patch.md`, and the boot note names it.
- `labor.md`: where the tokens of batches 8 and 9 went (14.6M): the fixed start of every agent 19.5%, the agents' own thinking 27%, checking roles 43% against rung workers 37%, exploration beyond the brief about 10% of a worker, 29% of what agents read already given to an earlier agent of the batch; eight levers, together about 1M to 1.5M a batch.
- The first designs for batch 10's goals, `design-batch10-fable.md` (about 5.2M) and `design-batch10-opus.md` (about 4.3M on Opus), from `design-batch10-brief.md`. They are not blind: the record's section 1 carried batch 9's cost by stage, its section 3 lines of the pipeline, POSITIONS and the build-cache note parts of it, and the Opus designer read the record's sections 6 to 8 by a paging slip. Both kept workers, skeptics and a repair round and cut the stages after the rungs.
- The explainer page comparing them with the pipeline and the token measurement: https://claude.ai/artifact/Wy1hJLharoRXVa2uZsr2m6 (source in the coordinator's scratchpad, `design-compare/index.html`).
- The shared-start cache question re-measured (FACTS, "The Workflow harness runs two agents at once on this box"): only a whole identical prompt is read from the cache; a prompt differing in its last line is written whole again.

## Pending, in order

1. The blind rerun of the two designs is done (Pavol's "Yes, run it. Blind rerun. Go.", shortly before 08:00 UTC): a content-only brief written by Sonnet (`blind-brief/`: `content.md`, `requirements.md`, `machine.md`; no pipeline word, no past cost; the per-site list's file left out by the word rule; CLAUDE.md reached the designers, a leak that cannot be removed), and two designers reading only that, the source, the specification, the ledger and `explorations/repo-internals.md`, choosing their own tiers. `design-batch10-blind-fable.md` (`3095ef978`): nine sub-pieces in a pipeline, Fable implementing the three rule-restating edits, Opus the library repairs, crash traces and reviews, Sonnet every checklist, suite run and measurement; about 48 agents, 7.1M (Fable 1.6M), about 13 hours. `design-batch10-blind-opus.md` (`f7d66bcd4`): six implementers (C split three ways by file), a run log of code states that enforces nothing run twice, refuting reviewers beside merged background runs, fixes only where something was found, one gate, one squashed commit; Fable only for the hardest checker piece, Sonnet for every launch, collection, gate and landing; about 18 agents, 3.3M (Fable 0.28M), about 8.6 hours. Both raised requirement 1 for the library repairs (no corpus test can go red on a checker error in the interpreter's library until the switch-over); the record answers it: such a rung's test is the distance measurement, its before the last landed gate's tables (POSITIONS, "No re-measuring what the record holds."). The blind Opus design also found two content risks in batch 10: row 604's positive compiled test needs `ImmutableArray`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare, and W's new load check has the shape of `String`'s `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///` families, which must keep loading; both for the post-batch review to check.
2. The custom-agent-type cache probe after the session's process restarts (about 12:33 UTC; an agent type written mid-session is not registered until then): three agents of type `cache-probe` (`.claude/agents/cache-probe.md`, untracked), their first calls' cache reads; if the system prompt is shared, a keep-warm agent of the same type next; the fallback, one identical prompt for every agent with its own part fetched as a tool result.
3. After batch 10 lands: its measured cost by role; then the Fable comparison of the designs (the leaky and the blind) with batch 10 as run and `labor.md`, with what to change; the page updated with it.
4. The same two designers at the whole project's scope (microGPT compiled and fast), designs only.

## Waiting on Pavol

- The rule on engineering taste, drafted from `cache-sharing.md`: an obstacle gets an attempt to engineer around it and the price of its recurring cost before it is accepted as impossible. To be put to him as one line.
- The decisions the designs raise, merged on the page's section 7 (the merged-diff review's place, one Fable ruling for a contested finding, approvals with required corrections, Sonnet for the gate and landing, merge commits on `main`, among them); taken up with the comparison, not before.
